El Padrino no es una película: es un tratado audiovisual sobre la inevitabilidad del poder, la herencia y la corrupción moral disfrazado de cine de gánsteres. Coppola toma el sueño americano, lo estrangula con una corbata italiana y lo convierte en una tragedia shakespeariana donde la familia funciona simultáneamente como refugio y condena. Lo verdaderamente fascinante no es la violencia, sino la burocracia con la que se ejerce. Michael Corleone no desciende al crimen por ambición, sino por la lógica casi determinista de un sistema donde la ética termina subordinada a la sangre. Cada decisión parece una tesis sobre cómo el poder deja de ser una herramienta para convertirse en una identidad. La fotografía de Gordon Willis, conocida con toda justicia como "el Príncipe de las Tinieblas", no ilumina a los personajes: los juzga. Las sombras no son una elección estética, sino una declaración filosófica de que toda autoridad nace parcialmente oculta. Y Nino Rota compone una partitura que suena menos a música y más a un lamento histórico por una familia condenada desde el primer brindis. Decir que El Padrino es "una película de mafiosos" es como decir que La Odisea trata sobre un hombre que vuelve a casa. Es una reducción casi ofensiva. Lo que Coppola construye es un mito moderno donde el capitalismo, el honor y la violencia dialogan hasta volverse indistinguibles. Obra maestra. No porque sea perfecta, sino porque redefine el lenguaje con el que el cine habla sobre el poder.

Man sollte keine Angst davor haben, Klassiker der Filmgeschichte zu kritisieren, bloß, weil dieser von der Masse gefeiert wird. The Godfather ist so ein Beispiel. Man kann nachvollziehen, wieso er ein großes Publikum erreicht: Der Plot ist gefällig erzählt , die Figuren sind schlicht und die Bildsprache eingängig. Wir verstehen sofort, was Sache ist. Copolla lässt kaum Raum für Ambivalentes, auch Politisches hält er hier vollkommen raus. Dabei kann gerade das Mafia-Genre rasant über die Entstehung von Kapital erzählen, doch das geschieht hier nur randständig. Stattdessen verschafft man dem Publikum Zugang zum Film durch die nervende Betonung von Familienwerten – ja, The Godfather ist ein durch und durch konservativer Film. Die Schwermütigkeit und die Länge des Films ist dabei nicht mit einer anspruchsvollen Kost zu verwechseln. Im Gegenteil kann man es sich immer ganz warm und gemütlich machen, wenn Don Vito Corleone vor dem Bildschirm läuft: Hier wird zwar geschossen und gemordet, aber immerhin ist hier das patriarchale Familienmodell noch intakt. An einem Scoresese-Gangster-Film, geschweige denn an einem Coppola, kommt dieser nicht ran.

After watching some mafia based television, goodfellas, a bronx tale, the departed, and season 1 of the sopranos (only just started it), I can say this might be my least favourite. The whole film is pure dialogue, which don’t get me wrong it is very interesting and well written, I think the fact it’s all talk and nothing else, for three hours, leaves a part of me bored, especially when watching at 4am. For the first hour I was thinking that Al Pacino could actually impress me for once, but once again he proves to be emotionless and boring. He was definitely decent in this tho, and was far better than in the other films I have watched him star in. His ending was really cool as-well, and makes me a bit more excited for part2, where he is the ‘Godfather’ or whatever. I can see why people rate this five stars, but I just don’t think that three long dragged hours of pure talk can cut it for me. A product of its time. So many of the characters were so surface level for a fucking 3 hour long movie! I've unironically seen better character building over the course of 40 minute CW serials. I didn't find even Al Pacino that interesting/endearing, let alone any of the female characters. Don Corleone was the most interesting and complex to me, and I liked him - but unlike Tony Soprano, they didn't care to explore the moral implications and repercussions of his lifestyle. The people we see them kill are Bad and Evil and one-not and he Loves His Children and is Tough But Fair. The pacing was weird - I couldn't tell what the final act was leading up to, and then apparently it was the assassination of some randoms we've had 2 minutes of prior screentime of and who I couldn't feel the symbolic weight of anyways, by anonymous shooters we've never seen before. (That's not to say I didn't greatly enjoy mass-murder-baptism scene - in fact it was probably my favourite, in isolation - and I do appreciate that it represented a greater symbolic act of revenge for his brother's death, but it still didn't work for me.) And then we end with a brooding Al Pacino lying to his girlfriend who has no personality besides Pretty and I did not care about, and therefore fully adopting the new "don" role, becoming the new Godfather. And then a door slams. I guess. As the credits were rolling I was just left thinking... that's it? Where was the fallout, the consequences, for all that death and drama? Please, just one meaningful consequence? This pacing can only be justified if they were always intending on making a "Part II" to continue the story, because on its own it just feels incomplete to me. It was undeniably cinematically well-made and I recognise probably, to me, a victim of the "classic movie which was ground breaking and iconic for the time and was the first to do all these cool things that have now been done better a million times over and I take for granted" problem. Same as "Taxi Driver". But I'm not a film critic, I'm only going to review a movie taken on its own merit, and to me... I don't know. The themes were interesting...? I guess? The idea of Business getting conflated with the Personal was a throughline. Again, I've seen the revenge plot done better since. I recall enjoying the first part - the plot was well set up and the villains mysterious and threatening. But then they all just... die. With the fall-out captured in a five minute long montage of newspaper headlines. New villains appear, and then they die too. And this valiant "that's my familys work not mine" war hero just... flips, and becomes a mafioso the second he gets back from like a month max of exile in Italy where the most significant thing he did was watch his Italian wife get blown up in a car for no reason after having genuinely more dialogue with her father than her and then immediately forgetting about her. There's no consequences, no explicit moral reckoning, for what was supposed to be that climatic act of killing the men who shot his father earlier in the film. He doesn't even have one panic attack! The battered sister is used as a plot point and a pawn to advance the more important sophisticated business of mafia men. Even at the end when she's hysterically yelling at Pacino "you never even considered me [when you killed my abusive husband]" it's like... yeah, he didn't, in multiple ways. If he wasn't aware of his violence, he didn't care how she'd be affected by losing her loving husband, and if he was aware of his violence, that wasn't even the reason he killed him! He didn't care that she was being abused, he cared that he was part of some complex behind-the-scenes murder plot of him. That never went anywhere because everyone gets killed! Like, I get it. It was the 50s, who cares about women, but why include DV as a plot point - going so far as to have a too-long scene of a man chasing his pregnant wife around their house with a belt while she screams, and then beating her - and then just stomp on it? Maybe that was the point, that by the end of the film Pacino is just so far gone into the moral grey of the mob that he doesn't care and that's a bad thing. That would make it more interesting, but not necessarily better. He is explicitly positioned as the protagonist and yet shows so few positive qualities throughout the whole film. I just don't buy his character degradation, if that was the intention. These flat, tired depictions of women just cheapen any movie they're in. If you zoom out, you realise all you're watching is the product of a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking about a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking. Just jerk eachother off already. We want to believe the Author is this unbiased surveyor and imitator of the human condition, and that reckoning - it brings them down to earth for me. How brilliant can a man or his story be if they don't trascend or even attempt to transcend the cruelty and primitivism of their era? Oh well. It's fun to get all the Sopranos references now. Maybe watching that first was setting this film up for failure because there's so much more room over 6 seasons and 50+ hours for real, conscientious character development and moral complexity and getting attached to not just the people but the world being built, than a movie, even one as long as this. We know from Gay Talese’s book Honor Thy Father that being a professional mobster isn’t all sunshine and roses. More often, it’s the boredom of stuffy rooms and a bad diet of carry-out food, punctuated by brief, terrible bursts of violence. This is exactly the feel of “The Godfather,” which brushes aside the flashy glamour of the traditional gangster picture and gives us what’s left: fierce tribal loyalties, deadly little neighborhood quarrels in Brooklyn, and a form of vengeance to match every affront. The remarkable thing about Mario Puzo’s novel was the way it seemed to be told from the inside out; he didn’t give us a world of international intrigue, but a private club as constricted as the seventh grade. Everybody knew everybody else and had a pretty shrewd hunch what they were up to. The movie (based on a script labored over for some time by Puzo and then finally given form, I suspect, by director Francis Ford Coppola) gets the same feel. We tend to identify with Don Corleone’s family not because we dig gang wars, but because we have been with them from the beginning, watching them wait for battle while sitting at the kitchen table and eating chow mein out of paper cartons. “The Godfather” himself is not even the central character in the drama. That position goes to the youngest, brightest son, Michael, who understands the nature of his father’s position while revising his old-fashioned ways. The Godfather’s role in the family enterprise is described by his name; he stands outside the next generation which will carry on and, hopefully, angle the family into legitimate enterprises. Those who have read the novel may be surprised to find Michael at the center of the movie, instead of Don Corleone. In fact, this is simply an economical way for Coppola to get at the heart of the Puzo story, which dealt with the transfer of power within the family. Marlon Brando, who plays the Godfather as a shrewd, unbreakable old man, actually has the character lead in the movie; Al Pacino, with a brilliantly developed performance as Michael, is the lead. But Brando’s performance is a skillful throwaway, even though it earned him an Academy Award for best actor. His voice is wheezy and whispery, and his physical movements deliberately lack precision; the effect is of a man so accustomed to power that he no longer needs to remind others. Brando does look the part of old Don Corleone, mostly because of acting and partly because of the makeup, although he seems to have stuffed a little too much cotton into his jowls, making his lower face immobile. The rest of the actors supply one example after another of inspired casting. Although “The Godfather” is a long, minutely detailed movie of some three hours, there naturally isn’t time to go into the backgrounds and identities of such characters as Clemenza, the family lieutenant; Jack Woltz, the movie czar; Luca Brasi, the loyal professional killer; McCluskey, the crooked cop; and the rest. Coppola and producer Al Ruddy skirt this problem with understated typecasting. As the Irish cop, for example, they simply slide in Sterling Hayden and let the character go about his business. Richard Castellano is an unshakable Clemenza. John Marley makes a perfectly hateful Hollywood mogul (and, yes, he still wakes up to find he’ll have to cancel his day at the races). The success of “The Godfather” as a novel was largely due to a series of unforgettable scenes. Puzo is a good storyteller, but no great shakes as a writer. The movie gives almost everything in the novel except the gynecological repair job. It doesn’t miss a single killing; it opens with the wedding of Don Corleone’s daughter (and attendant upstairs activity); and there are the right number of auto bombs, double crosses, and garrotings. Coppola has found a style and a visual look for all this material so “The Godfather” becomes something of a rarity: a really good movie squeezed from a bestseller. The decision to shoot everything in period decor (the middle and late 1940s) was crucial; if they’d tried to save money as they originally planned, by bringing everything up-to-date, the movie simply wouldn’t have worked. But it’s uncannily successful as a period piece, filled with sleek, bulging limousines and postwar fedoras. Coppola and his cinematographer, Gordon Willis, also do some interesting things with the color photography. The earlier scenes have a reddish-brown tint, slightly overexposed and feeling like nothing so much as a 1946 newspaper rotogravure supplement. Although the movie is three hours long, it absorbs us so effectively it never has to hurry. There is something in the measured passage of time as Don Corleone hands over his reins of power that would have made a shorter, faster moving film unseemly. Even at this length, there are characters in relationships you can’t quite understand unless you’ve read the novel. Or perhaps you can, just by the way the characters look at each other.

Critiquing a movie with this much gravitas almost feels like internet suicide, but I’m gonna do it anyway. First of all, I’m happy this movie exists solely for the truckload of entertainment it has provided to me via all the media it has inspired. It is and always will be an absolute classic, and I’m honored to have finally seen it. But, judged on its own merits today, stacked up against a genre which it helped birth, I have to say, I didn’t like it. There are parts which I really liked, but they are too few and too far between. You know how some movies are three hours long yet they feel barely two? Well, The Godfather is a three-hour movie and feels like six. "Bloated" was the first thing that came to my mind when the credits rolled. Its insistence on showing you the mundane, dragging the hell out of it, and beating you over the head with it is truly something special. The plot points which should drive the story forward feel very unsatisfying. All the time that could have been spent on better character development is spent in the most inconsequential of all places, which hardly matters at the end of the day. And even though Al Pacino's presence and charisma is one of the few reasons why I stuck around until the end, his performance is still fairly plain—far removed from his best. Sadly, the biggest crime The Godfather has committed is that it must have been so good and influential when it came out that all the copycats have eventually caught up. All of the genre tropes have been done better a million times since, producing far more compelling stories than what the Corleone family has to offer today.

A long overdue rewatch has only cemented, in my mind, The Godfather’s right to its legendary and seminal status. Aside from the obvious and needlessly stated praises, there are a few things I picked up on and enjoyed thoroughly that I’m not quite sure I noticed on my first watch. I’m a huge fan of the obliviousness to which the women of the Corleone family (whether connected via marriage or blood) default to in order to maintain their comfort, regardless of the atrocities they are surely aware of happening around them constantly. That last moment where Kay is crying and asks Michael whether it’s true that he’d ordered the executions of the heads of the five families, and he simply responds “no” after some behaviour that clearly denotes “yes” - her reaction to that, falling into his arms and smiling in relief, it’s incredible to watch. That “no” that holds back so much pain from truths she knows exist just for the sake of comfort, it’s perhaps the best moment of “no wonder mafia enterprises worked” I’ve ever  seen from a mobster movie. I’m also a huge enjoyer of Michael’s acceptance of the godfather role being portrayed quite literally as he becomes the godfather for his sister’s child - simple but impactful writing. Beautifully realised and a fantastic culmination of 70s noir swagger with unexpected aspects of realism.
